all the way down and around

Intelligence, from the physics of a bit up, and around again.

An engineer's walk through what sits under intelligence: down through the whole stack (physics, devices, architecture, systems, algorithms, learning) and around three of them: the classical one that runs on transistors and GPUs, the brain, and the quantum computer.

How to walk a step

For every substantial step, keep one page:

  1. Problem. What were they trying to solve, and why then?
  2. Objects. The mathematical objects involved.
  3. Mechanism. The central idea, in my own words.
  4. Assumptions. Which still shape how we think today?
  5. The math behind it. The one equation or argument the idea rests on, worked through once, and only as far as the idea needs.
  6. One experiment that can be reproduced.
  7. One rival explanation. What experiment would tell the authors' explanation apart from another one for the same result?
  8. Next question it raises, with links to earlier steps.

Keep an analogy apart from a mathematical equivalence, and an empirical observation apart from a theorem.

At any layer of any stack, ask:

  • Compute. What operation, at what precision, and how many per joule?
  • Store. Where does the state live, for how long, and what does it cost to keep or erase a bit?
  • Move. How many bytes travel per useful operation, and who sees a write, and when?
  • Search. What space is being searched, and how is it indexed, pruned or approximated?

Two readings from each of the 15 chapters, in order: one pass across every approach before going deep in any. Do the task at each station before moving on.

00

What we're building

What counts as intelligence, and how would we know?

  • ↗

    One page. General methods that scale with compute have won, again and again. Keep it in mind for the whole list, then argue with it.

    task
    Choose a scaling result and state which resource increased and how performance changed.
    references
    • The work itself essay
    connections
  • ↗

    Intelligence as efficiency at acquiring new skills, not skill itself. The origin of the ARC benchmark.

    task
    Read the definition of skill-acquisition efficiency. Compare two learners with equal final scores but different prior experience.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections

Sutton bets on general methods that scale; Chollet measures how efficiently a system acquires new skills. Which of them do today's language models vindicate?

01

Experiments & evidence

How do you know a result about an AI system is real?

  • ↗

    Evaluations are experiments, so treat them as such: standard errors, clustered questions, paired comparisons and power analysis for language model evals.

    task
    Take a benchmark score of 72% on 500 questions. Compute its standard error, then say how many questions you need to tell 72% from 74% reliably.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections
  • ↗

    Rebuild the ImageNet test set from scratch and accuracy drops by 11 to 14 points, yet the ranking of models barely changes. What a benchmark does and does not measure.

    task
    Say why the models lost accuracy but kept their order. Decide whether that is evidence of overfitting to the test set, and what would distinguish the two explanations.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections

Take one result from another chapter. What would you need to see (samples, seeds, held-out data, a baseline) before you believed it?

02

Information & compression

Is prediction the same as understanding?

  • ↗

    Entropy, coding and n-gram language models. Cross-entropy loss and next-token prediction come straight from here.

    task
    Read the section on entropy. Calculate the entropy per symbol of independent flips with a 3:1 bias.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections
  • ↗

    Prediction is compression: a language model with arithmetic coding beats gzip, even on images and audio. Shannon and Solomonoff applied to LLMs.

    task
    Turn a log-loss in nats per token into a compressed size for a 1 MB text. Say why the size of the model has to be counted.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections

If prediction is compression, what does skill-acquisition efficiency add that a compression ratio misses?

03

Learning from data

Why does fitting the training data generalise?

  • ↗

    Networks memorise random labels yet generalise on real ones. Classical theory alone can't explain it.

    task
    Read the random-labels experiment. Say which classical generalisation bounds it rules out, and why explicit regularisation does not rescue them.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections
  • ↗

    Double descent: past the interpolation point, bigger models get better again.

    task
    Sketch test risk against capacity past the interpolation threshold. Say what the minimum-norm interpolant has to do with the second descent.
    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections

Which explanation predicts the second descent, and which would have predicted the random-labels result?

What should a model assume about its input?

11

Scale & cost

What does intelligence cost to compute, and who pays?

  • ↗

    Loss falls as a predictable power law in parameters, data and compute. This turned AI into an engineering and capital problem.

    task
    Read the loss curves for model size, data and compute. State what is held fixed in each comparison.

    • The work itself paper
    connections
  • ↗

    The table to remember: reading DRAM costs hundreds of times more energy than an add. Moving data costs more than computing on it.

    references
    • The work itself paper
    connections

Take one model you know. Is its training limited by compute, by memory bandwidth or by energy, and which reading tells you?
